introduction-the-ci-pipeline-is-a-weapon.core: CI pipelines hold the keys to production (cloud credentials, signing keys, deploy rights) and run code from many sources. Compromising one is like stealing a factory's master key.

first_principles.problem: Attackers target CI (Codecov, SolarWinds, malicious PRs) because one foothold reaches every environment.
truths: They execute third-party code (actions, deps, PRs).
Secrets in CI are exposed to every step.

analogy.title: A factory master key
analogy.story: Stealing one worker's badge opens one room; the master key opens everything.
analogy.breaks: Perfect isolation is costly, so tier your protections by risk.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Every step in CI can read what the job can read.

check.q: Why are CI pipelines high-value targets?
check.a: They hold privileged credentials and execute third-party code, so a compromise reaches every environment.

the-curl-bash-anti-pattern.core: Piping a downloaded script straight into a shell runs unreviewed, mutable remote code with the job's full privileges. Pin, verify and review what you run instead.

first_principles.problem: An installer script on a vendor's site is modified by an attacker, and every pipeline that curls it executes the malware.
truths: Remote content can change at any time.
There's no integrity check in a pipe.

analogy.title: Reading a sealed envelope aloud on stage
analogy.story: You don't know what's inside, and you've committed to saying it before you can check.
analogy.breaks: Checksums only help if they come from a trusted, separate channel.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A tampered download fails the checksum, and nothing runs.

code.text:
curl -fsSLo tool.tgz https://dl.example.com/tool/v1.8.2/tool-linux-amd64.tgz
echo "3b1f...e9  tool.tgz" | sha256sum -c -
tar xzf tool.tgz

check.q: What's the core danger of `curl | bash`?
check.a: It executes mutable, unverified remote code with the job's full privileges.

runner-isolation-handling-untrusted-buil.core: CI for public PRs runs code written by strangers. Run it on ephemeral, isolated runners (or sandboxes like gVisor or Firecracker) with no secrets and no network path to internal systems.

first_principles.problem: A fork PR modifies the build script to read secrets or plant a backdoor on a persistent self-hosted runner.
truths: Untrusted code can do anything the runner allows.
Persistent runners keep state between jobs.
derivation: Give fork PRs **no secrets** (the default on GitHub).
Use **ephemeral** runners: one job, then destroy.
**Segment the network** away from internal systems.

analogy.title: A quarantine lab for unknown samples
analogy.story: Unknown samples go in a sealed lab with no access to the main building, and the lab is sterilised after each use.
analogy.breaks: `pull_request_target` runs with secrets in the base repo's context, which is a common hole if you check out PR code.

example.title: An open-source project's CI
flow: Fork PR → hosted ephemeral runner, no secrets
example.outcome: untrusted builds can't reach anything valuable.

check.q: Why is pull_request_target dangerous with a PR checkout?
check.a: It runs with base-repo secrets and write permissions while executing untrusted PR code.

oidc-federation-death-to-long-lived-keys.core: Instead of storing static cloud keys in CI, the job presents a short-lived OIDC token signed by the CI provider. The cloud trusts that issuer and exchanges the token for temporary credentials scoped to that repo and branch.

first_principles.problem: Long-lived AKIA keys in CI secrets leak, never expire and grant broad access.
truths: CI platforms can sign identity tokens per job.
Clouds can trust external identity providers.
Short-lived credentials limit the damage of a leak.
derivation: Register the CI provider as an **OIDC identity provider** in the cloud.
Create a **role** trusting it, with **conditions** on repo and branch.

analogy.title: A visitor badge issued at reception
analogy.story: Instead of a permanent key, you show ID and get a badge valid for one floor, for one hour.
analogy.breaks: Loose trust conditions (any repo, any branch) undo the benefit.

example.title: GitHub Actions → AWS

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: There's nothing to leak or rotate, and only main can deploy.

code.text:
permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy-prod
      aws-region: eu-west-1
# trust policy condition: token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub = repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main

example.outcome: CI has keyless, scoped, short-lived cloud access.

check.q: What claim should AWS trust policies restrict for GitHub OIDC?
check.a: The `sub` claim, limiting access to a specific repo (and branch or environment).

secrets-management-beyond-environment-va.core: Env-var secrets leak through process listings, child processes, crash dumps and accidental `env` output. Fetch secrets just-in-time from a vault, scope them per job and environment, mask them, and prefer files or short-lived tokens.

first_principles.problem: A debug step runs `env` and prints every secret into logs that many people can read.
truths: Every process in the job inherits env vars.
derivation: **Fetch at runtime** from Vault or a secrets manager with OIDC auth.
Pass via **files with tight permissions** when possible.
**Mask** them, never echo them, and **rotate** regularly.

analogy.title: A hotel safe vs. cash on the dresser
analogy.story: Cash on the dresser is visible to anyone who walks in; the safe opens only when needed.
analogy.breaks: Masking is best-effort. Transformed secrets (base64) can still leak.

example.title: Fetching a DB password from Vault

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The secret exists only for this job, and access is audited in Vault.

code.text:
- uses: hashicorp/vault-action@v3
  with:
    url: https://vault.acme.io
    method: jwt
    role: ci-migrate
    secrets: secret/data/prod/db password | DB_PASSWORD

example.outcome: secrets are short-lived, scoped and auditable.

check.q: Why are environment variables risky for secrets?
check.a: Every child process inherits them, and they easily end up in logs or crash dumps.
